questions.explanation: Reuse is what turns a single exposure into a portfolio problem, and the arithmetic is worth spelling out: if a person uses one secret in thirty places and it appears in a list of ten thousand pairs, that one secret gives a party up to thirty services from a list entry that cost nothing to obtain. It is also why a stored value that resists guessing does not help here, since the party is not guessing, they are presenting something that is correct. The second option is the belief that strong protections are the answer, and they are not, because no per-site mechanism can tell that this particular secret is one the owner has used before. The last one is worth naming because a second factor is the reliable answer to reuse and it is not the same value everywhere, which is exactly the property that makes it work.
questions.hint: Ask what the party has, and then ask how many places that single thing is accepted.
questions.learningObjective: explain why reuse turns one compromise into many

answer.exemplar: The two weaknesses are found by different means because the artefact that carries them is different. The first is in the source, so it is the same defect in every copy of that version, it is found by reading or analysing the code, and the repair is a change to the code followed by a deployment. The second is not in the source at all: the same build is sound in one deployment and exposed in another, which means a code review will pass it, and a scan of the shipped defaults will pass it too, because the value that matters is the one the deployer chose. So the review has to compare what is running against what is intended, artefact by artefact and deployment by deployment, and the artefact of record becomes the configuration rather than the repository. The practical consequence is that the fix and the verification are different too: setting the option back is a change to a running system, it can be undone by the next deployment that re-applies the old value, and confirming it worked means reading the setting on the host rather than trusting the change record. Which is exactly why a configuration weakness tends to come back after a successful fix, and why the durable repair is a checked-in definition of the intended settings plus a comparison at deploy time.

questions.explanation: Classifying the weakness decides which review method can find it, which is why the classification is worth the argument. A weakness in the code is a property of the artefact that is built, so every copy of that version carries it and a source-level review reaches all of them at once. A weakness in the settings is a property of one running system, so no amount of reading the source or scanning the shipped defaults will produce it, and the review has to compare the running state against the intended state. The deeper consequence is about persistence: a code repair survives the next deployment because it is in the artefact, whereas a setting can be silently re-applied by an old process, which is why this class of weakness tends to return after a fix that appeared to work.
questions.hint: Ask which artefact carries each weakness, and therefore which method could ever find it.
questions.learningObjective: explain what changes about a review when the weakness is in the settings

answer.exemplar: A rule that has spoken nothing all year has produced no information, because silence is the same observable whether the estate is quiet, the rule's condition is too narrow for what really happens, or the feed it depends on has stopped. All three look identical from the alert panel, and only the first is a statement about the system being watched. The consequence is that coverage has to be established deliberately rather than inferred: confirm the feed is still arriving and that recent entries match the fields the condition reads, then confirm the condition would actually match something that has happened. That second half is the part most often skipped, and it can only be done with a known example, so the practical exercise is to take an event that is known to have occurred, take one that is known not to have occurred, and check what the rule does with each. If it is quiet on both, the rule is measuring nothing and the year was unobserved rather than uneventful. The same reasoning applies to any control whose evidence of working is its absence of output, which is why a monitoring estate gets its own review with its own inventory.

questions.explanation: This is a question about what an observation can support, and the answer is that silence supports nothing without a separate check on the observer. The rule's condition and its data feed are both assumptions about the world, and either can stop holding while the panel keeps looking healthy, so a year of no output is consistent with a year of no events and with a year of no looking. Coverage is therefore an assertion that has to be produced, and the way to produce it is to run the rule against events whose occurrence is already known in both directions, which is the only way to distinguish a quiet estate from a blind one. That is a review of the monitoring itself rather than of the monitored system, and it is a step that is skipped precisely because the dashboard looks fine.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be true of the rule for a quiet year to mean a quiet estate.
questions.learningObjective: explain why an unfired rule is not a measurement

answer.exemplar: Least privilege acts on the second half of a risk, so it is worth being exact about which half and why. An identity that has been taken is a fact about the world that no grant review can change: whoever holds it will present it, and the sign-in will accept it exactly as it accepts the legitimate owner. What a grant review changes is the size of what the identity can do once it is accepted, and it changes it directly, because the list of permitted actions is what the system consults on every single one of them. That is why the mechanism is described as containment rather than prevention: the same entry still succeeds and the same account still signs in, but the sequence of actions available afterwards is shorter and each one leaves a smaller mark. Three practical consequences follow from taking that seriously. First, the benefit is proportional to how wrong the original grant was, so a review that finds nothing to remove has found a system that was already narrow and has bought very little. Second, it composes with everything else rather than replacing it, since a narrow grant limits the damage of a stolen identity while a second factor decides whether the identity is stolen at all, and the two are independent jobs. Third, it is one of the few controls whose effect can be verified by reading, because the granted rights are a list somebody can check against the job description, which is also why a grant that nobody claims is the usual place the investigation starts.

questions.explanation: The whole effect of least privilege runs through the impact half of a risk score, and the reason is mechanical rather than rhetorical: a permitted-action list is consulted at the moment of each action, so narrowing it shortens the sequence available to a misused identity without touching whether that identity can sign in. This is why the principle is described as containment, and why a team that has done a grant review and then relaxed its sign-in requirements has given away the half it did not work on. The second consequence is that the control composes rather than substitutes, since it bounds what happens after a compromise while other layers decide whether a compromise happens, and a third is that it is verifiable by reading, since the granted rights and the job description can be compared without running anything.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two halves of a risk this control moves, and what it never touches.
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism by which least privilege bounds impact

questions.explanation: The order runs from evidence to change to confirmation, and skipping the first step is what makes these projects fail. A grant is usually justified by what somebody asked for, and requests accumulate, so the list of what a job needs has to come from watching the job rather than from the history of requests, which is a record of what people believed. The comparison then produces a candidate list, and the important word is nothing: a right no current workflow touches is a candidate for removal, not a certainty, since quarterly work and holiday cover are exactly the uses that a two-week observation misses. Removal is a live change to a running system, so it is done with a way back, because the alternative is that a team which is afraid of breakage never removes anything. The final re-check is what turns a one-off tidy into a control, and it is the step that gets dropped once the project is called finished.
questions.hint: Ask which step produces the evidence the next step depends on.
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a least privilege review

options.text: Read what each job actually does, from the work itself rather than from the request
Compare the rights in use against that list and write down the ones nothing uses
Remove the unused rights, watching the work and keeping a way to put one back quickly
Re-check the list after a few weeks of real use and keep what was needed

questions.explanation: Containment is first because every hour of delay is another hour in which the party can act, and the constraint on it is that it must not destroy evidence or leave a foothold intact by accident. Understanding follows, since without knowing how they got in and what they reached, the removal is a guess and the recovery may reopen the same door. Removal is third, and the phrase about a known state is the point: cleaning what was touched is not the same as confirming nothing else was, and a system that cannot be shown to be in a known state is rebuilt rather than cleaned. Recovery is fourth and starts by changing the affected identities, since restoring the service with the same working secrets restores the party's access along with it. The write-up is last and it is the only step that makes the next one cheaper, which is why it is the first thing dropped when the pressure is on.
questions.hint: Ask which step stops the clock, and which step needs to know how the party got in.

Work out how they got in and what they reached, from the records that exist
Remove what let them in and rebuild or clean the affected parts to a known state
Bring the service back with the affected identities changed and the entry closed
Write up what happened and change the process so the same step is caught earlier

answer.exemplar: Hardening and removal act on different quantities, and that is the whole argument. Hardening reduces the number of ways into a component that is still there, so it leaves the parser, the configuration, the unpatched code and the maintenance obligation in place, and every weakness later found in that component is a new item on the same list. Removal deletes the component, so the whole class goes with it: nothing to reach, nothing to patch, nothing for a future scan to find and nothing for a future party to try. The second-order effect is the one that usually decides it, which is that a rarely used service is under-maintained precisely because it is rarely used, so the hardening effort is also a promise to keep doing this, and a promise nobody re-checks is the weakest control there is. The second question is the honest part of the answer, because removal is not automatically right. It is right when nothing genuinely needs the component, or when a replacement exists that meets the need without a new exposure of its own. Hardening wins when the service performs something no other thing does and the cost of removing it falls on people rather than on risk, and in that case the decision should be recorded as accepted with a review date, because the case for hardening depends on the patch staying possible and on somebody continuing to believe it. What does not win either way is the third option: leaving it running unreviewed on the argument that it is hardly used, since hardly used describes the demand rather than the reach.

questions.explanation: The comparison is between reducing a number of ways in and removing the thing that has them, and the second is a different order of improvement rather than a slightly better version of the first. Hardening leaves behind a component that must be patched, monitored and re-hardened as new weaknesses appear, which is a recurring cost proportional to how rarely the component is used, since rare use is what makes it easy to forget. Removal has a one-off migration cost and no recurring cost at all, which is why it wins whenever a replacement meets the need. The honest counterweight is that removal is not always available, since a service that does something nothing else does cannot simply be deleted, and in that case the decision is a recorded acceptance with a review date rather than a claim that the system is now safe.
questions.hint: Ask whether hardening removes the recurring obligation or only reduces it.
questions.learningObjective: explain the argument for removal over repair
